text: In course 10 you built a FinOps tagging taxonomy — keys like cost-center, environment, and owner, each with an agreed set of values. That taxonomy is genuinely useless if it lives only in a wiki page. Once tagging is merely recommended, some resources get tagged correctly, some inconsistently, and some not at all, and a cost report built on that data is wrong in ways that are hard to even notice. Tagging has to be enforced at the point resources are created, inside the landing zone, the same way a network boundary is.

Azure Policy has built-in definitions for exactly this: requiring a tag, or requiring a tag and its value, assignable with a Deny effect at the same management group scope from Lesson 17. With Deny in place, a resource missing cost-center simply can't be created — the deployment fails at apply time, not three months later when the cost report shows an unexplained untagged line item. Policy can also inherit a tag value down from a parent scope automatically, which solves a different problem than just requiring the tag exist.

AWS splits this the same way it split policy enforcement in Lesson 17. A tag policy defines allowed keys and values across an organization and reports on resources that don't comply — detective, not preventive, on its own. The preventive half comes from an SCP that denies resource-creation calls unless a required tag is present, using the aws:RequestTag condition key. Pairing the two mirrors Azure exactly: one blocks at creation, the other catches whatever slipped through.

Here's what breaks quietly if a tag is only required to be present, not constrained to known values: platform-team, Platform Team, and platform_team end up as three different strings describing the same team, and every cost report that groups by cost-center now splits that team's real spend across three rows. That's why enforcement pairs a Deny-if-missing rule with an allowed-values list, so the tag isn't just present — it's one of a known set a dashboard can actually group by.

Because the taxonomy is now enforced by policy defined in Terraform and read by chargeback reporting finance depends on, a change to the schema — a new required key, a renamed allowed value — is an architecture change with consequences for every team under that scope. It belongs in a reviewed pull request, not a Slack message asking people to start using a new tag going forward. Treating the taxonomy as governed infrastructure is what keeps cost governance from quietly rotting.
